paragraphs.en: By the end of my third [[week]] in the lab I was [[stressed-out]], sleeping badly, and unable to explain my own project without a diagram.
The work was [[technical]] in a [[way]] I had not expected: hours of cleaning data, checking cables, and re-running the same test.
My supervisor said the results were [[unclear]] rather than wrong, which I took as a small mercy.
At night I sat in my [[cottage]] and read old papers [[online]] until the screen hurt my eyes.
It was [[extremely]] quiet out there, and I felt [[uncool]] and slightly ridiculous among the confident students of the institute.
The [[elder]] of the group, a professor who had studied vision for thirty years, [[presided|preside]] over our Monday meeting with a [[strict]] calm.
She [[offered|offer]] me a place on the team studying visual [[perception]], and I [[accepted|accept]] before she finished the sentence.
Her [[technique]] was [[old-fashioned]] but precise, and she insisted that we learn the [[technic]] of asking small questions.
[[Access]] to the scanner was limited, so we booked it in [[slots|slot]] of two hours and often worked [[late]].
Language was a [[barrier]] at first; when I could not explain myself, I learned to [[hide]] my panic behind a joke.
Our experiment asked whether the [[subconscious]] mind can notice a change in an [[image]] before the eyes report it.
A small [[electronic]] device made a [[beam]] of light [[vibrate]] at a fixed rate, and a camera recorded the response.
The brain's [[neural]] activity was noisy, and every cough in the corridor could [[distort]] the signal.
We [[generated|generate]] [[thousands|thousand]] of trials to fix a [[baseline]], then compared each new trial with it.
The change was [[rapid]] but tiny, and it took months to [[harness]] it into a result we could trust.
The lab next door kept a [[captive]] [[rat]] that had lived there longer than most students.
It was an [[omnivore]] with a taste for [[raisins|raisin]] and a tail like a small [[brush]].
Its diet was kept to a strict [[ratio]] of fat and protein, and its data was [[pure]] enough to publish.
I once brought it a spoon of [[cream]], which was against the rules and [[worth]] the risk; the [[raid]] on the fridge felt like a small crime.
The [[staple]] of its diet was dry grain, which it would [[lay]] in a corner and guard for hours.
A [[net]] over the cage kept it from escaping, and there was no [[shortcut]] to cleaning it; someone had to [[care]] for it every day.
My [[neighbour]], a farmer with a gray [[beard]], owned forty [[acres|acre]] of flat land behind my [[cottage]].
He [[hauled|haul]] [[lumber]] in an old truck and [[burned|burn]] brush at the edge of the field every autumn.
The [[weather]] that month was [[harsh]]: hot days, cold nights, and a wind that never stopped.
The truck could barely [[bear]] the weight of the wood, and he drove it slowly, as if he had all the time in the world.
Sometimes I heard him singing [[far-off]] songs in a language I could not place, and I wondered about the [[geography]] of his life.
The [[neighbor]] on the other side said the farm was haunted, though she had never seen the [[ghost]]; the [[homeowner]] laughed and said ghosts do not pay rent.
Each spring [[thousands|thousand]] of birds [[migrate]] through the [[Netherlands]], and an [[environmentalist]] group [[counts|count]] them.
The local [[government]] wanted to widen the road, which the group saw as a threat to a [[rare]] species.
A [[lawmaker]] proposed a [[permanent]] ban on night traffic, but the farmers called it an [[onerous]] [[punishment]].
At the hearing the environmentalists were [[overwhelmingly]] in favour, while the truck drivers were not.
The two sides had become [[foes|foe]], and [[neither]] would move.
I went to the hearing out of curiosity, and the [[debate]] was stranger than I expected: one speaker said the road would [[harm]] the birds, and another said the birds would simply move.
Both claims were [[rational]] on the surface, but each rested on a [[base]] of half-finished evidence.
The chairman [[struggled|struggle]] to [[justify]] a decision that would please nobody, and his [[just]] tone only made the room angrier.
It was [[absurd]], really: a [[string]] of numbers had [[pulled|pull]] two villages apart, and no one could say where [[justice]] lay.
I sat [[alongside]] a young mother who said the whole argument needed a [[punch]] of honesty, and I wrote that down.
Back at the [[office]], the lab's finances were worse than the road debate.
Our grant had been [[underfunded|underfund]] for a [[decade]], and the department carried a [[debt]] it could not repay.
We had to [[cope]] with old equipment and [[deal]] with suppliers who charged by the hour.
The [[cost]] of a new sensor had [[skyrocketed|skyrocket]], and the company could no longer [[manufacture]] the old part, so my [[purchase]] request sat on a desk for weeks.
A [[corporation]] offered to sponsor us [[via]] its foundation, but only if we used their software, which felt like a trap.
The old scanner needed a full [[overhaul]], and in our [[haste]] to [[save]] money we had stopped maintaining it; the whole situation was an [[indictment]] of how science is funded.
A [[veteran]] science writer visited the [[studio]] to record a short talk for the radio.
She had spent her [[career]] avoiding [[fame]], and she spoke in a [[manner]] that made complicated ideas sound simple.
Her [[style]] was [[elegant]] but plain, and her [[layout]] for the script left no [[blank]] space.
She said a good script should sound like speech, not like a [[copy]] of a textbook.
The studio was [[stuffy]], so she asked for the window to be opened.
Before the interview she warned me about [[buzzwords|buzzword]]: they make a sentence sound scientific without making it clear.
Her [[vocabulary]] was wide but never showy, and she [[paraphrased|paraphrase]] every hard term before using it.
I tried to [[imitate]] her, and the result was a stiff little paragraph that [[said|say]] nothing.
She read it, laughed, and told me to say it out loud first and write it down second.
My [[parent]] used to give me the same advice about letters, and I had forgotten it.
On Wednesday I taught a group of [[undergraduates|undergraduate]] how to run the basic test.
They were quick and careless, and one of them [[unplugged|unplug]] the machine while it was recording.
I had to [[strip]] the ruined data and start again, which took the whole afternoon.
Their questions were better than their technique, and one of them [[corrected|correct]] a mistake in my code.
One asked whether the [[study]] would ever produce a real [[improvement]] in medicine, and I said I hoped so.
The department was [[awaiting|await]] news of the grant renewal, and the [[second]] review had not yet arrived.
I emailed the funding office to [[inquire]], and received an automatic reply.
The reply said the committee would meet soon, which is what it always says.
A postdoc told me the wait was the worst part of a scientific career.
We kept working [[steadily]] in the meantime, because stopping was not an option.
In June I was invited to a conference abroad, and the paperwork was [[cumbersome]].
The [[visa]] form asked for details of every trip I had taken in ten years.
I filled it in twice, made a [[copy]], paid the fee by [[card]], and mailed it with a photograph I did not like.
Two weeks later I [[got|get]] a message saying the visa was ready, and I carried it in my [[purse]] like a small passport.
At the airport I sat [[aboard]] the plane beside a [[teenager]] in a [[very]] old jacket.
He asked where the sea ended, and the plane began to [[march]] down the runway before I could answer.
The conference hall was full of [[parallel]] sessions, and I could not decide which talk to attend.
A [[laureate]] gave the opening lecture on the physics of music and the mathematics of rhythm.
She argued that beauty is not a decoration but a [[core]] part of scientific thinking, an [[unconventional]] claim in that room.
Her talk had no slides and no [[scale]] on any axis; she simply played a recording and let the light [[die]] behind the screen.
I wanted to [[weep]] and could not say why, and [[far]] from home I felt both free and weightless.
At my poster, a stranger asked a hard question about the baseline and would not accept a vague answer.
I felt the old panic in my chest, the one that used to [[stun]] me in seminars.
Then I remembered the professor's advice: answer only what you can measure.
We ended up talking for an hour, and he offered to [[swap]] data with our lab.
He said science advances when rival groups [[unite]] around a shared [[element]] of doubt, a view I found hard to [[accord]] with at first.
That evening I walked along a canal, and the [[scene]] was so calm that I could hear the [[beat]] of my own heart.
On Saturday I visited an exhibition that tried to [[launch]] a dialogue between artists and scientists.
A [[generous]] donor had given the museum a small [[ruby]], a [[bunch]] of fossils, and a [[carrier]] full of old slides.
The curator argued that [[mankind]]'s [[survival]] depends less on clever machines than on the [[rate]] at which we learn to share knowledge.
She was a vocal [[advocate]] of open data, [[whereas]] the university wanted to keep its results private.
One exhibit, a [[weak]] projector behind a sheet, offered a [[reinterpretation]] of the moon landing as a [[fantasy]] about collective hope.
The room was [[cool]] and quiet, and a thin man with an athlete's [[physique]] stood [[on]] a chair to fix the machine, ignoring the [[intrusiveness]] of the museum's cameras.
I asked the curator what [[genre]] the exhibition belonged to, and she said it belonged to none.
She said every generation must [[strive]] to explain science in its own language, or the explanation will [[wear]] thin and become a slogan.
In the worst [[scenario]], she added, people stop asking and simply trust whoever shouts loudest.
The lab, the road, the farm, and the museum were all asking the same question in different words.
